<reason>Side B built the stronger path to victory by defending the binding timetable as the only mechanism capable of breaking the coordination deadlock (chicken-and-egg) in green fuel investment. B credibly neutralized A's feasibility and equity critiques through the phased-flexibility design (expiring exemptions that maintain the obligation) and pre-committed transition finance for vulnerable states. While A made a compelling case against premature mandates and for carbon pricing, A's alternative failed to fully answer the critique that price signals alone cannot guarantee the simultaneous infrastructure build-out required, and A's clipped closing slightly weakened the final crystallization.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 2 answers to A's pressure questions, demonstrating how a phased mandate with bankable, expiring availability exemptions and pre-funded rebates maintains regulatory bindingness and investment signals while avoiding cliff-edge scarcity and uncompensated immediate harm to import-dependent nations.</best_rebuttal>
